text:
This section examines Experiment E —
Failed all-positions neural redesign

from first principles. Keep two questions
separate: does changing the

order change the measured outcome, and
does the proposed search

method beat a matched alternative at the
same distinct-evaluation budget?

Hypothesis: deepening XOR and parity to
five functional permuted layers

would increase useful order variance.
Setup: 60 generations; deeper plain

stack; 50–100 training-step budget.
Result: variance fell to exactly zero;

all stage-one orderings remained at chance
accuracy 0.500. Important

contradiction: the stochastic search still
surfaced best fitness 1.0,

exposing best-ever noise inflation.
Decision: reject the plain deeper stack

and redesign with residual blocks. Visual:
all landscape points collapse

onto a flat 0.5 line; a false “1.0 best”
spike

is revealed as a noisy measurement, then
stamped “benchmark rejected.”

Now read evidence panel E-flat. The axes,
units, and sample

are stated on screen. The sample
represented here is the

sample reported in the source. Raw
observations remain visible wherever

the artifact provides them. Censored
observations stay marked at the

cap rather than becoming invented hitting
times, and sampled landscapes

leave unobserved permutations blank. The
supported finding is: Result:

variance fell to exactly zero; all
stage-one orderings remained at

chance accuracy 0.500. The broader claim
not established here is:

The conclusion is scoped to the recorded
evaluator, landscape, and

budget. This evidence changed the program
as follows: Decision: reject

the plain deeper stack and redesign with
residual blocks. The

distinction is part of the result. A large
ordering effect

does not automatically imply an
evolutionary-search advantage, and

almost-sure convergence does not promise
practical efficiency.
